extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, translators, and literary critics; educated readers interested in standards for poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for judging and composing poetry and drama: how metre, diction, plot, character-ideality, translation fidelity, and dramatic probability contribute to artistic success. Includes criticisms of contemporary (German/English) practices and examples (Don Juan, Milton, Lessing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic effect from cadence and paragraph sweep
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief effect of poetry is produced by cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs: e.g. “with many a winding bout Of linked sweetness long drawn out,” rather than in the even flow or the prominence of isolated, antithetic single lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value prolonged cadential movement and the sustained architecture of lines/paragraphs. Single-line vigour is often injurious to the total effect unless introduced for some specific purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use single-line vigour only with purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Prominent, antithetic single lines are 'indeed injurious to the total effect, except where they were introduced for some specific purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat striking one-line moments as intentional accents; avoid scattered single-line epigrams that disrupt the larger cadential sweep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the spirit/genius of each language in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each language has its particular spirit and genius; translations must not 'sacrifice' the idiom of the target language to the original (criticising Voss for doing violence to German idiom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating, adapt to the idiom and spirit of the target language rather than slavishly imitating source-language forms; avoid importing foreign idioms that wound native diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful translation: avoid additions and omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A bad translation may contain 'pages on pages not in the original--and half the original was not to be found in the translation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations should be faithful to the original's content (no invented passages) and avoid omitting substantial portions; fidelity of content matters as much as stylistic fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and line-length adapt to language
rubrics_metrics.description: A Greek or Latin heroic line can often be rendered in German as one line, but in English typically requires 'a line and a half' of our common heroic metre; the count of syllables, not strict line parity, is the operative measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt metrical translation to the prosodic norms of the target language; expect differences in line economy between languages and translate for equivalent rhythmic/syllabic effect rather than literal line-for-line correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of plan and structural design in long poems/odes
rubrics_metrics.description: The author 'values himself upon the plan of his odes' and accuses modern lyrical writers of gross deficiency in this respect; long poems benefit from a thoughtful overarching plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give careful attention to the formal design and plan of extended poems (odes/epics). Structure and unity of design are virtues; composing only in 'favourable moments' without plan risks incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate appropriation of source-material when skilful
rubrics_metrics.description: Old romances and books may be treated as 'a sort of common property, from which a man was free to take whatever he could make a good use of'; Wieland's 'thefts' are defended when exquisitely managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowing is permissible provided the appropriation is skillful and transforms sources into something artistically valuable; skilful adaptation can be a legitimate creative method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria of good drama (Lessing's virtues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing's dramas exemplify excellence in 'the construction of the plot; the good sense of the sentiments; the sobriety of the morals; and the high polish of the diction and dialogue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drama by plot construction, soundness of sentiment, moral sobriety, and polished diction/dialogue. These are preferable to mere irregularity or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: 'German drama' formed by sensational mixture
rubrics_metrics.description: The so-called German drama (as criticised) is an 'olla podrida' mixing bloated styles, morbid sensibility, horrific incidents, ruined castles, dungeons, trap-doors, skeletons, and perpetual moonshine—popular but denounced as cramps of weakness and sickly imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware combining sensational Gothic ingredients without depth; such mixtures produce superficial excitement rather than true artistic merit. Avoid relying on horror-ornamentation and exaggerated incident as substitutes for structure and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character ideality: balance of the generic and the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal consists in 'the happy balance of the generic with the individual'—the generic makes the character representative and instructive; the individual gives it living interest. Quotation: 'Forma formans per formam formatam translucens' as definition of ideal art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters that are simultaneously symbolic (representative of types/classes) and vividly individualized; avoid making figures mere abstractions or mere portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability through harmony: permit suspension of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet need not make the audience literally believe impossible incidents; he must create a dramatic probability by ensuring the whole work is in harmony so the audience yields to a dream with eyes open and judgment postponed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish internal consistency and tonal/structural harmony across the work so the audience will accept extraordinary incidents or superhuman characters without being jarred; dramatic probability is earned by total coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extravagant incidents acceptable if unified by harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The extravagance of incidents and the super-human agency of a character (e.g., Don Juan) prevent the wickedness from shocking the mind when the whole is coherently idealized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the work's tone and design justify extravagance, extreme incidents can be artistically effective; ensure they are integrated into the idealizing vision so they do not merely shock or disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest derives from intellectual superiority in characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare’s male characters and figures like Don Juan or Milton’s Satan attract us because of their intellectual lordship and superiority to fear of the invisible world; the coexistence of great intellect with guilt excites strong interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intellectual superiority as a source of tragic or sublime interest—characters whose intellect or daring subordinates ordinary fears can be powerfully attractive on stage or page; craft such portrayals carefully to avoid glorifying vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great poets should elevate readers rather than pander
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'the province of a great poet to raise people up to his own level, not to descend to theirs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to expand readers' or audiences' sensibility and understanding rather than merely catering to prevailing tastes or lowest common denominators; artistic ambition and challenge are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in representation: avoid fashion or trick on venerable subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion and trick wound our veneration for poets and great men (example: powdered periwigs on old men are 'disgusting'); 'The author of THE MESSIAH should have worn his own grey hair.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing venerable figures or subjects, prefer authenticity over contemporary fashion or artifice that undermines dignity; small affectations can injure perception of greatness.
